This is a problem for users who cannot see the image (e.g., screen reader users) and in situations where the image fails to load. Which WCAG criterion does this violate? WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.1.1 (Non-text Content) requires that all non-text content that is presented to the user has a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose. The criterion states: "All non-text content that is presented to the user has a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose, except for the situations listed below." In this case, the image is non-text content and lacks an alt attribute. Therefore, it fails SC 1.1.1. Note: The exception situations in 1.1.1 include controls, input, time-based media, test, sensory, CAPTCHA, decoration, etc. However, without any context, we cannot assume the image is purely decorative. Even if it were decorative, best practice is to use an empty alt attribute (alt="") to indicate that the image should be ignored by assistive technology. Since the alt attribute is missing entirely, it is a failure. Therefore, the answer is 1.1.1. Answer: 1.1.1 The HTML fragment `` violates **WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.1.1 (Non-text Content)** because: - The image lacks an `alt` attribute, which fails to provide a text alternative for non-text content. - Without `alt`, screen readers announce the image filename or a generic placeholder, which does not convey equivalent information to users who cannot see the image. - This directly contradicts SC 1.1.1, which requires text alternatives for non-text content unless the image is decorative (in which case `alt=""` must still be used). **Answer:** 1.1.1
